study.title: Isaiah 40 - Comfort, greatness of God, and renewal of those who trust in him
study.overview: Isaiah 40 opens a new section marked by comfort after the discipline of the people. The chapter announces that the pain of exile is not the final word: God forgives, restores and prepares a new beginning. The prophetic voice calls to prepare the way of the Lord, proclaiming that the glory of God will be revealed and that his word abides forever. Then the text contrasts the human fragility, the vanity of idolatry and the incomparable majesty of the Creator. The chapter ends with a very concrete promise: those who trust the Lord receive renewed strength to continue their journey.

outline.title: Comfort and preparation for the coming of the Lord
outline.explanation: The prophet receives order to speak tenderly to Jerusalem, announcing forgiveness, end of punishment and restoration. Then a voice calls for the way of the Lord, with images of leveling that express the removal of obstacles to the manifestation of divine glory.

outline.title: Human fragility and the good news proclaimed
outline.explanation: A voice calls upon that all flesh is like grass: human life is transient, but the word of God remains forever. Zion must proclaim with courage that the Lord comes with power, with retribution and pastoral care, governing with justice and meekness.

outline.title: The incomparable God and the worthlessness of idols
outline.explanation: The text accumulates rhetorical questions to show that no one measures, advises or teaches God. The nations are small before him, and the idols made by artisans are ridiculous and unable to help, whether for rich or poor.

outline.title: The sovereign Creator who sustains the tired
outline.explanation: The prophet recalls that God is the Creator who reigns over the earth, humbles rulers and does not tire. Still, he strengthens the tired. The chapter ends with the promise of renewal for those who trust in it: they will go up, run and walk without exhaustion.

study.context: The given notes place Isaiah 40 on the horizon of Babylonian exile and the hope of restoration. In this reading, the prophet speaks as one who announces comfort to a people already wounded by judgment, announcing that the time of discipline has been shut down and that the deliverance of God is approaching. The chapter is also read by the notes as having an importance that surpasses the return of captivity, for it points to the saving coming of the Lord.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the restoration of the people begins with God's forgiveness and initiative, not with human merit. Holiness and divine majesty appear in the radical difference between the Creator and the creatures: everything that is human passes, but the word of the Lord remains. The text also fights idolatry by showing that any image made by human hands is an empty replacement of the living God. In contrast to the powerless idols and the passing rulers, God is presented as sovereign, pastor and sustainer of the weak. The final promise is not an absence of weakness, but the renewal of forces to persevere in confidence.

scholarViews.insight: The promise that those who trust in the Lord renew their forces are linked to the powerful image of the eagle and recalls a divine ransom that awakens hope for the people.
The so-called "falai to the heart of Jerusalem," is understood as a message of encouragement and reconciliation for a downcast people, stating that God's mercy is still reserved for him.
The beginning of the chapter is seen as a message of consolation addressed to the people in captivity, announcing that the time of favor and deliverance is already approaching.

questions: In which areas of my life have I acted as if my way was hidden from the Lord, as Israel did in verse 27?
What forms of "idolatry" today still try to replace trust in the living God with things made by our own hands or efforts?
How can I depend on God in a practical way to receive new forces and keep walking, rather than just trying to resist alone?
study.practice: This week, choose an area where you are tired or discouraged and turn it into a specific prayer of trust. Instead of repeating only that it is difficult, declare before God that he does not tire, that his word remains and that he can renew his strength. Also try to encourage someone with words of comfort, not of recovery, remembering that God restores the slaughtered and sustains the weak.
study.uncertainty: The notes received allow to safely affirm the background of Babylonian exile and some interpretive connections with the coming of the Messiah and with John the Baptist, but this study avoided developing these connections beyond what was explicitly mentioned. There is also a textual note in Adam Clarke about verse 7, indicating handwritten variations; therefore, no doctrine was built from this observation. Some applications are pastoral inferences consistent with the text, not independent historical statements.
